events.title: Charif Shanahan Poetry Reading
events.description:
November 04

5:00PM - 6:30PM

Poet Charif Shanahan will read from a selection of their work.

Charif Shanahan is the author of two collections of poetry: Trace Evidence: poems, which was a finalist for the National Book Critics Circle Award in Poetry and longlisted for the National Book Award for Poetry; and Into Each Room We Enter without Knowing, which was a finalist for the Lambda Literary Award for Gay Poetry and the Publishing Triangle's Thom Gunn Award. He is an Assistant Professor of English at Northwestern University. Shanahan’s poems appear widely, in such journals as The Nation, The New Republic, The New Yorker, The New York Times Magazine, The Paris Review, and PBS NewsHour. His work has been anthologized in American Journal: Fifty Poems for Our Time (Graywolf Press, 2018), Furious Flower’s Seeding the Future of African American Poetry (Northwestern, 2019), and African American Poetry: 250 Years of Struggle & Song (Library of America, 2020).Shanahan is the recipient of the Whiting Award; a National Endowment for the Arts Literature Fellowship; a Wallace Stegner Fellowship in Poetry; a Fulbright Senior Scholar Grant to Morocco; and residency fellowships from Cave Canem Foundation, Hawthornden Foundation in Griante, Italy, the MacDowell Colony, La Maison Baldwin in St Paul, France, and the Robert Rauschenberg Foundation, among other awards and recognitions.

events.title: Daniel Goldmark: “The Televised Animated Musical Extravaganza”
events.description:
November 06

3:00PM - 4:00PM

You’re invited to hear a talk about music in shows like The Simpsons, Family Guy, the Bugs Bunny/Roadrunner Show, Muppet Babies, Animaniacs, and South Park by Daniel Goldmark.

Professor Goldmark learned to play piano at age 5 because of a song he’d heard in a cartoon. He went on to work on music at a Hollywood animation studio, produce recordings of cartoon music for a major record label, and become a pioneering scholar of music and animation. He’s written seven books about cartoons, films, and popular music, including the foundational monograph on cartoon music, Tunes for ‘Toons: Music and the Hollywood Cartoon (2005). A professor of music at Case Western Reserve University, he is the director of their Center for Popular Music Studies and teaches classes on animation, music, and film.

About the Presentation

From the earliest sound cartoons, musical performances have been a ubiquitous part of American animated shorts. By the 1940s, however, the popularity of such performances had waned, and they largely disappeared by the 1950s. Limited budgets and limited animation—exemplified most famously in Hollywood by the output of the Hanna-Barbera studio—meant a hiatus for musical numbers, until the animation renaissance of the late 1980s and early 1990s, when The Simpsons, Animaniacs, South Park, and other series reintroduced musical moments as a regular feature of cartoons. Unlike the theatrical shorts of the 1930s, where musical numbers were an accepted and expected component of the cartoon universe, television cartoons used such performances as a way to refer to other prevalent forms of pop culture, including Broadway, film musicals, and even their own animated ancestors. But the style and approach to performing musicals have changed remarkably little in all that time. Even when Hollywood animation was at its least remarkable (in the 1970s and 1980s), the connection to the 1930s style never entirely disappeared, so that when the animation renaissance occurred, the musical and all its trappings was waiting right there to be brought back into the service of the cartoon.

Sponsored by the Department of Film, Media, and Digital Studies, the Department of Music, and the McGaw Lecture fund from the Public Lectures Committee.

events.title: Yuraq Qaqa: Indigenous Engineering and Mapmaking Before the Inka in the Colca Valley of Highland Peru
events.description:
November 17

7:30PM - 8:45PM

Carved boulders and outcrops depicting agricultural terraces, irrigation channels, and reservoirs—referred to as maquetas—have been found in multiple highland regions in the Andes, especially the Colca Valley. In 2024, our team found a maqueta, known locally as Yuraq Qaqa (white rock in Quechua), a massive 7,000 m3 carved outcrop of rhyolitic tuff making it among the largest documented maquetas to date in the Andes. With funding from a 2025 Archaeological Institute of America Site Preservation Grant, we have been documenting and working with the community to preserve this unique site. Yuraq Qaqa attests to centuries of agricultural experimentation, innovation, and knowledge production prior to Spanish colonization of the Colca Valley. While other known maquetas depict relatively circumscribed terrace and irrigation systems, Yuraq Qaqa serves as a regional map of mountains, glaciers, and agricultural systems that encompass not just the valley, but much of the region of Arequipa. Yuraq Qaqa is also unique in its incorporation of abstract artistic elements, including circles, spirals, and rectilinear petroglyphs, which challenge western forms of cartographic knowledge. Taken together, Yuraq Qaqa suggests communities in the Colca Valley engaged in regional-scale environmental engineering and coordination between communities in the centuries before Inka expansion.

About the speaker: Lauren Kohut (Ph.D., Anthropology, Vanderbilt University) is an Assistant Professor of Environmental Studies and Anthropology at Winthrop University. As an archaeologist and anthropologist, she is interested in the complex interactions between humans and their environment across deep time scales. Her research investigates how periods characterized by social and ecological crisis–like warfare, climate change, and colonialism–disrupt and transform society. Since 2004, most of her research has taken place in the Peruvian Andes where she has been engaged in long-term field research. Her research has been supported by the Archaeological Institute of America, the National Science Foundation, and the Wenner-Gren Foundation.

events.title: Archeology Series Presentation Tess Davis, “Blood Antiquities: Tomb Raiders, Art Smugglers, and the Black Market in Cultural Treasures”
events.description:
January 26

7:30PM - 9:00PM

We all know the thrill of tomb raiding adventure novels and Hollywood films—Indiana Jones, Lara Croft, Thomas Crown—hunting for hidden treasures. But the real stories of looted and trafficked cultural property are far darker. In reality, it’s no longer daring explorers who dig up the past, but opportunistic criminals, war profiteers, mafia networks, armed insurgents, and even terrorist organizations.

The Antiquities Coalition, founded in 2014 by Deborah Lehr, was created to combat this cultural racketeering. As a “think and do tank,” the Coalition unites business leaders, government officials, lawyers, security experts, and other professionals in working towards a future when the past is preserved for the next generation, not looted, smuggled, and sold to the highest bidder.

In this exclusive talk, Executive Director and attorney Tess Davis takes you behind the scenes to reveal the high-stakes, illicit world where stolen art and cultural treasures fuel crime, conflict, and corruption—and the ways we can fight back.

About the speaker: Tess Davis, a lawyer and archaeologist by training, is Executive Director of the Antiquities Coalition. She oversees the organization’s work to fight cultural racketeering and also manages the day-to-day operations of the institute’s staff in Washington, DC, as well as programs overseas. Davis has been a legal consultant for the Cambodian and US governments and works with both the art world and law enforcement to keep looted antiquities off the market. She writes and speaks widely on these issues. In 2015, the Royal Government of Cambodia knighted Davis for her work to recover the country’s plundered treasures, awarding her the rank of Commander in the Royal Order of the Sahametrei.

events.title: History’s Kelley Lecture Featuring Judy Giesberg - Listening to a Very Loud Archive:  The Last Seen Project’s 5000 Stories of Slavery and Survival
events.description:

This talk will highlight the collaborative work of students and scholars to recover and archive the stories of formerly enslaved people’s search for family after freedom. It will introduce readers to the Last Seen Project Archive of more than 5000 information wanted and lost friends’ advertisements published in Black-owned newspapers after the Civil War. Each ad tells the story of a family separated in slavery and their search for one another afterwards. The talk will take listeners along on a journey of discovery of this little-known history and explain its significance to our understanding of the nation’s past—and present.

events.title: Archeology Series Presentation: Carter Clinton, “Soil Genomics: Ancestry, Health, and Community-Engaged Science”
events.description:
February 16

7:30PM - 9:00PM

Carter Clinton is a genetic anthropologist, is an Assistant Professor at N.C. State University, where he directs the Ashes (Ancestry, Soil, Health, and Evolutionary Studies) Lab. His research integrates ancient DNA, burial soil genomics, and African diaspora population genomics to investigate ancestry, identity, and health in African American communities. His lab pioneers non-destructive metagenomic methods that recover human, microbial, plant, and pathogen DNA from burial soils without disturbing ancestral remains. Current work applies evolutionary medicine and whole-genome sequencing to identify ancestry-derived disease markers associated with complex diseases, immune gene variation, and cardiometabolic conditions leveraging temporal comparisons between pre-admixture burial soil genomes and living descendant communities to build ancestry-informed frameworks that move beyond race as a biological proxy. A National Geographic Explorer and Cosmos Scholar, he centers descendant communities as active research partners across all phases of his work.

events.title: Davidson College Theatre Dept. Nora: A Doll's House
events.description:
April 07

7:30PM - 9:30PM

Plays in the Barber Theatre

Nora is the perfect wife and mother. She is dutiful, beautiful and everything is always in its right place. But when a secret from her past comes back to haunt her, her life rapidly unravels. Over the course of three days, Nora must fight to protect herself and her family or risk losing everything.

Henrik Ibsen's brutal portrayal of womanhood caused outrage when it was first performed in 1879. This bold new version by Stef Smith reframes the drama in three different time periods. The fight for women's suffrage, the Swinging Sixties and the modern day intertwine in this urgent, poetic play that asks how far have we really come in the past hundred years?

Suitable for ages 12 and up.
